catalog_quote: 1.2. The Intonation. Intonation is very important in order to speak Pokot language well. The intonation is often the only difference between two given words, while the phonems are the same. The intonation helps to distinguish: The singular form of a noun from its plural. The accusative case of a noun from the nominative case. The subject from the object in a sentence. The meaning of a word. This is very common in the verbs. ... Types of tones. In Pokot language there are four types of tones: a High tone. Transcribed in this book as "´". b Low tone. For which we do not write any symbol. c High-low tone. ... d Low-high tone. ... The combined tones ( c,d.) make the vowel a bit longer. They appear above all in the dyptongues. ... Lionel Bender (eds.), Nilo-Saharan: Proceedings of the First Nilo-Saharan Linguistics Colloquium, Leiden, September 8-10, 1980, 19-39. Dordrecht: Foris. tone_statements.quote: 4, PAKOT 4,1 TONAL PROCESSES There are three underlying tonemes (H, L, F). There is no downdrift, no automatic downstep, and no downglide of final low tones. ... Fall Simplification Falling tones are generally (except in very slow and deliberate speech) converted to high tones. ... As in Markweta, a simplified fall will downstep a following high tone. ... 4,2 NOMINAL MORPHONEMICS There are three underlying (and surface) stem types (L, H, F), and two primary suffix types, L (type "a") and H (type "b").
tone_statements.locator: pp. 29-31, section 4 'Pakot' (4.1 Tonal processes opening p. 29; Fall Simplification and Fall Commutation Downstep p. 30; 4.2 Nominal morphonemics p. 31); F defined in Appendix A pp. 36-37 as 'high falling tone (high to low)'.
tone_statements.summary: Pakot: three underlying tonemes high, low, falling; no downdrift or automatic downstep; falls mostly simplify to high and downstep a following high; high is realised rising after low.

tone_statements.citation: Bennett, Patrick R. 1974. Tone and the Nilotic case system. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 37(1): 19-28. DOI 10.1017/S0041977X00094817.
tone_statements.quote: In a number of Nilotic languages spoken in East Africa it has been shown that there exists formal marking of case based exclusively on tonal differentiation. This has been fully described in Maasai (Tucker and Mpaayei, 1955) and all investigated Kalenjin dialects (Tucker and Bryan, 1962. 1964–5). It also is clearly present in my own data on Teso, though interestingly enough it seems to be lacking in the Luo group generally.
tone_statements.locator: abstract (Cambridge Core landing page), article pp. 19-28
tone_statements.summary: Kalenjin dialects incl. Päkot: nominative case marked solely by tone (tonal case), per Tucker & Bryan's Päkot data; no tone inventory given in the abstract.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in copies we hold at the stated places (Herreros Baroja 1989 pp. 11-12 page scan; Beech 1911 pp. 49-50 djvu text). (2) The classification 'tonal (four tones, lexical + grammatical; no stress rule stated)' rests on a 1989 missionary/learner grammar, which is not a linguist's phonology, but it is one of only two full grammars of Pokot, the only open one, and its content (H, L, HL, LH; tone marks number, case, verb class) agrees with everything known about Kalenjin prosody (Tucker & Bryan, Creider, Rottland, Dimmendaal all analyse Kalenjin lects as tone languages with tonal case).
